text: Cattle are ruminants with a complex digestive tract able to produce energy and protein from forages and fiber such as straw. The rumen is a large fermentation chamber of over 100 liters, packed with bacteria, protozoa, and fungi — roughly 10 to 50 billion bacteria and 1 million protozoa per ml of rumen fluid. A healthy cow's rumen contracts 1–2 times per minute, mixing its contents, bringing microbes into contact with new feed, and moving material along. Different microbes specialize in digesting fiber, starch, or protein. In this fermentation, fiber, starch, and sugar are broken down into fatty acids and gases (carbon dioxide and methane) — the cow absorbs some fatty acids directly as energy (for movement, milk, meat) while some energy feeds the microbes themselves, which multiply and are later digested as a protein source; the gas produced is eliminated by belching. For protein: dietary protein or urea is broken down by rumen microbes into ammonia, which the microbes use (with energy) to multiply into a mass that is about 80% protein and passes to the intestine for full digestion; some leaf proteins bypass this microbial breakdown and go directly to the intestine ('bypass protein').
